extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and educated readers of Romantic-era literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and evaluative principles for writing and judging drama and poetry, with emphasis on plot construction, diction, translation, ideal art, and the balance between the generic and the individual in characterization. Drawn from Coleridge's literary criticism (Biographia Literaria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total rhythmic effect over isolated lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefers cadences and the sweep of whole paragraphs (“with many a winding bout / Of linked sweetness long drawn out”) rather than the prominence of antithetic vigour in single lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single, antithetic, vigorous lines are 'injurious to the total effect' except where introduced for some specific purpose. Aim for an overall flowing cadence across larger units of diction rather than seeking striking lines at the expense of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use single-lines only for specific purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Antithetic vigour of single lines can harm the total effect unless they serve a clearly intended function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve pointed, isolatable lines for moments of deliberate emphasis or structural need; avoid frequent isolated epigrams that break the sustained musicality of longer passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and authenticity in portrayal
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men and poets should be thought of 'as parts of nature'; anything of trick and fashion wounds the reader’s perception of their greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affectations, fashionable artifices or theatrical trappings (illustrated by the criticism of powdered periwigs) when presenting characters or historical figures; such artifice undermines dignity and verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect each language’s spirit in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each language has its particular spirit and genius; translations must not sacrifice the target language’s idiom to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue line-for-line literalism if it violates the idiom and spirit of the target language. Coleridge notes German lines often concentrate meaning differently than English; translators should adapt to the receiving language's capacities rather than force foreign structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid borrowing foreign idioms injudiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing idioms from another tongue is 'a very dangerous practice'; Milton often injured his prose and verse by this liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer native, pure diction (Dryden's prose is recommended as a model of 'pure and native English'). Use foreign turns sparingly and only when they genuinely serve expressive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of coherent plan and structure (especially in odes/long poems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Value placed on the plan of odes; Klopstock 'values himself upon the plan of his odes' and accuses modern lyrical writers of gross deficiency in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a clear structural plan for lyrical and long-form works. A thought-out plan elevates lyrical composition above formless or episodic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing’s excellence lies in the construction of the plot; construction is a primary merit in dramatic works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot is well-constructed and coherent. Plot architecture should support moral and psychological truth rather than serve merely sensational incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good sense of sentiments and sobriety of morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued qualities in Lessing’s dramas: 'the good sense of the sentiments; the sobriety of the morals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic sentiment should be measured and morally sober—avoid overwrought or mawkish ethical posturing that undermines seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polished diction and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: High polish of diction and dialogue is praised as an excellence (again cited of Lessing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for refined, apt language in dialogue and diction; polish contributes to dramatic authority and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensational stagecraft and pandering to low tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatrical barbarisms—horses, dogs, elephants, and other zoological rarities—and 'Kotzebuisms' in morals and taste are condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist relying on cheap spectacles or sensational devices to draw audiences; aim to restore classical or higher standards rather than pandering to base curiosities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bloated style, morbid sensibility, and gothic excess
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called German drama is criticized as a compound of 'bloated style', 'strained thoughts', 'loaded sensibility', and 'horrific incidents' (ruined castles, dungeons, trap-doors, skeletons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assemble an 'olla podrida' of overblown sentimentalism and gothic contrivances. Maintain proportion, probability, and taste; avoid excessive reliance on sensational incident and morbid inwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability via harmony of the whole work
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may solicit the audience 'to yield ourselves to a dream'—a dramatic probability sufficient for pleasure can be created if the whole work is in harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a play contains implausible or supernatural elements, ensure they are integrated harmoniously so the audience can willingly suspend disbelief. The unity and internal consistency of the piece produce dramatic credence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal art: balance of generic and individual elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal consists in the 'happy balance of the generic with the individual': the generic makes a character representative and instructive; the individual gives living interest and reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting figures, balance archetypal (representative) qualities with distinct individual detail. Avoid making characters mere abstractions or mere portraits; both aspects are necessary for ideal art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character intelligibility and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters (e.g., Don Juan, Milton’s Satan) should be intelligible abstractions and maintain a consistent character to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make character motivation and agency understandable even when elevated or idealized. Preserve consistency—extreme traits (power, wickedness) must cohere psychologically throughout the work to maintain dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intellectual power in characters to generate attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakespeare’s male characters are attractive because they are 'cast in the mould of Shakespeare’s own gigantic intellect'; superiority to fear of the invisible world is especially dazzling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray intellectual superiority or independence (e.g., fearlessness regarding the unseen) with care—such traits can draw the audience and create intense dramatic interest if credible within the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful borrowing and intertextual appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wieland’s 'thefts' are praised as 'so exquisitely managed' that 'the greatest writers might be proud to steal as he did'; old romance materials may be treated as common property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intertextual borrowing is permissible and can be admirable when handled with taste and skill. Rework shared myths or motifs creatively rather than copying clumsily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forced metrical affectation and pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Later faults ascribed to Schiller: 'studied feebleness of interest', 'diction elaborately metrical', 'the affectation of rhymes', and 'the pedantry of the chorus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not employ artificial metrical tricks, forced rhyming, or pedantic choruses that call attention to manner rather than meaning. Let metrical choices arise from expressive need, not from mannered fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke genuine emotion rather than cheap sentimentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the power of exciting tears is 'highly rated', it is 'easy' and 'done every day by the meanest writers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for authenticity and depth in emotional effect; avoid facile devices that prompt tears without artistic justification. True pathos should arise from character and situation, not contrivance.
